analysis.one_liner: Gives student loan borrowers bankruptcy rights, debt collection protections, and loan cancellation for public service.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to four House committees on the day it was introduced, never advanced, and died when the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make federal and private student loans dischargeable in bankruptcy like most other debts, stop the government from taking Social Security benefits, tax refunds, or wages to collect student loans, bar colleges from withholding transcripts over a defaulted loan, and cancel half the balance for borrowers who make 60 payments and work five years in public service. It also excludes forgiven student debt from income tax and lets parents with PLUS loans use income-based repayment.
analysis.who_benefits: Tens of millions of current and former students, especially defaulted borrowers who lose wages or retirement benefits to collection, parents stuck on Parent PLUS loans, and public-service workers carrying large balances.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Student borrowers, especially those in default

how_it_helps.text: Lets borrowers wipe out student loans in bankruptcy by striking the special rule that shields them from discharge [S3].
Bars the government from collecting student debt by garnishing wages or offsetting Social Security, railroad retirement, black lung benefits, or tax refunds [S3].
Requires the Education Department to cancel half the interest and principal for borrowers who make 60 monthly payments and work a public service job for 5 years [S3].
Excludes discharged student loan debt from taxable income, so forgiveness does not trigger a surprise tax bill [S3].
Makes Parent PLUS loans eligible for income-based and income-contingent repayment plans [S3].
Stops a defaulted loan from being used in professional license proceedings and bars colleges from withholding transcripts or degrees because of default [S3].
Restores a six-year time limit on lawsuits to collect student loans, which currently face no limit [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers absorb the cost of cancelled federal loan balances, and private lenders, guaranty agencies, and debt collectors lose collection tools and the near-guaranteed recovery they have today.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers, private lenders, and debt collectors

drawbacks.text: The 50% cancellation after just 60 payments plus 5 years of public service would be a large, ongoing cost to federal taxpayers and could crowd out other education spending [S3].

Allowing all student loans, including private ones, to be discharged in bankruptcy with no hardship standard would likely raise interest rates on private student loans and shift losses to lenders' other borrowers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer protections are real and targeted at people already in financial distress, and the taxpayer cost is the price of the cancellation benefit. The design is generous: 50% forgiveness after only 60 payments is a bigger giveaway than the existing 10-year public service program, and full bankruptcy discharge without any hardship test goes further than most proposals. The protections against garnishing Social Security and withholding transcripts are hard to argue against; the cancellation formula is where the honest cost debate lies.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to four House committees on the day it was introduced, none of them ever acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Frederica Wilson introduced the bill on May 24, 2019, with no cosponsors [S1][S4][S5].
It was referred the same day to the Education and Labor, Ways and Means, Judiciary, and Oversight and Reform committees [S5].
No committee ever reported it, no vote was ever scheduled, and the 116th Congress ended January 3, 2021 with the bill still in committee [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private student lenders, guaranty agencies, and debt collectors kept their collection powers and the bankruptcy shield for student loans; defaulted borrowers gained nothing.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the bill's only sponsor was a Democrat and it drew zero cosponsors from either party in a House Democrats controlled.

industries.note: The bill strikes the bankruptcy carve-out that protects all student loans, letting borrowers discharge private loans like any other debt. Private lenders have relied on that shield since 2005 to charge higher rates with less default risk.

Bans wage garnishment and offsets of Social Security and tax refunds for student debt, and restores a six-year time limit on collection lawsuits, shrinking the near-guaranteed recovery these firms earn on defaulted loans.
Taxpayers fund the 50% cancellation after 60 payments and lose some collection tools, but also stop chasing debts from retirees and the destitute, which often costs more than it recovers.
Bars withholding transcripts or degrees over a default, removing leverage some schools use to push former students into paying, though schools face no direct financial hit.
